course.title: African History & Civilizations
course.description: A survey of the African past from the origins of humankind to the independent states of today, covering ancient Nubia and Aksum, the great West African empires, the Indian Ocean and Atlantic worlds, colonization, and liberation. It directly challenges the old myth that Africa had no history, treating the continent's many peoples with the seriousness their record deserves. Structure and facts adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: On which continent did the earliest human ancestors and our own species evolve?
questions.explanation: Fossil and genetic evidence places the origins of hominins and of Homo sapiens in Africa, which is why it is called the cradle of humankind.

questions.prompt: The West African ruler famous for a spectacularly wealthy pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 was…
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa, emperor of Mali, made a hajj so laden with gold that his spending is remembered along the route.

questions.prompt: The large dry-stone city in southern Africa built by Shona-speaking people is known as…
questions.explanation: Great Zimbabwe's massive mortarless stone walls were raised by ancestors of today's Shona between roughly the 11th and 15th centuries.

questions.prompt: In the 4th century the kingdom of Aksum, in the Horn of Africa, adopted which religion under King Ezana?
questions.explanation: Aksum became one of the earliest states to adopt Christianity, a heritage continued by the Ethiopian Orthodox church.

questions.prompt: The 1884-1885 conference where European powers set rules for carving up Africa was held in…
questions.explanation: The Berlin Conference formalized the 'Scramble for Africa' among European empires.

questions.prompt: The first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win its independence, in 1957, was…
questions.explanation: Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became independent in 1957 and inspired a wave of liberation across the continent.

questions.prompt: Across the Sahara, West African merchants chiefly exchanged their gold for which northern good?
questions.explanation: The trans-Saharan trade famously swapped southern gold for Saharan salt, along with copper, cloth, and books.

questions.prompt: The claim that Africa 'had no history' before Europeans arrived is best described as…
questions.explanation: Written records, archaeology, and oral tradition document deep African histories; the 'no history' claim is a prejudice long since rejected by scholars.

lessons.title: Out of Africa: the cradle of humankind and the land itself
lessons.grammar_note: Dates this deep are estimates with error bars. Treat 'about 3.2 million years ago' as a careful approximation from dating methods, not an exact year.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why Africa is called the cradle of humankind, and describe how the continent's geography shaped the societies that grew across it. You will be ready to connect physical features such as deserts, rivers, and grasslands to the ways people fed themselves and traded. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, on which continent did the earliest human ancestors evolve, and what kind of evidence could support that conclusion? Keep that answer in mind, because the rest of the course builds outward from these origins. Africa is not a single environment but dozens of them, and that variety is the first key to its long and layered past. By the end of this lesson you should be able to sketch, in plain words, both where humans came from and the stage on which African history played out.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The human story begins in Africa. Fossil and genetic evidence places the origins of the hominin family, and of our own species Homo sapiens, on this continent. Modern humans later spread from Africa to populate the rest of the world. Geography then set the terms for what followed. The Sahara, the largest hot desert on Earth, separates a Mediterranean north from the lands below, yet it was never an unbroken wall: trade routes crossed it, and in wetter ancient periods green corridors did too. Great rivers, the Nile, Niger, Congo, and Zambezi, watered farms and carried goods. Rainforest, open savanna grassland, highland plateaus, and long coastlines each supported a different way of life, from cattle herding to fishing to long-distance commerce. Slow shifts in climate, including the drying of a once-green Sahara, repeatedly changed where people could settle. To read African history well, picture this map first.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Among the most famous finds is 'Lucy,' a skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis discovered in Ethiopia and dated to roughly 3.2 million years ago. Early remains of Homo sapiens come from sites such as Omo in Ethiopia and Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, the latter dated to about 300,000 years ago, among the oldest known. The main dispersal of modern humans out of Africa is usually placed around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. During the African Humid Period, roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago, a 'Green Sahara' held lakes and grassland, and rock paintings at Tassili n'Ajjer record people herding cattle where only sand lies now. Researchers Mary and Louis Leakey, working at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, helped establish East Africa as central to the human origins story.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why do scientists call Africa the cradle of humankind? 2) Name two great African rivers and one thing a river provides to the people along it. 3) Was the Sahara always a desert? 4) About how long ago did modern humans begin spreading out of Africa? 5) What does rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer tell us about the past Sahara? Answers: 1) The oldest hominin and Homo sapiens fossils, plus genetic evidence, point to African origins. 2) Examples include the Nile, Niger, Congo, Zambezi; rivers give water for farming, fish, and transport. 3) No; during the African Humid Period it held lakes and grassland. 4) Roughly 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. 5) That people once herded cattle there, so the region was far wetter.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: imagining the Sahara as a permanent, impassable barrier. It has changed with climate and has always been crossed by trade. Mistake: treating Africa as one uniform landscape. Its deserts, forests, highlands, and grasslands are as different as separate continents, and that diversity drives its history. Mistake: reading 'cradle of humankind' as a slogan rather than a conclusion from fossils and genetics. Exit: (a) Name the find, from Ethiopia, dated to about 3.2 million years ago. (b) Give one reason the Sahara should not be thought of as a wall. Answers: 'Lucy,' an Australopithecus afarensis skeleton; it was green and settled in wetter periods and was always crossed by trade routes, so it linked rather than only divided.

lessons.title: The Nile and the Red Sea: Nubia, Kush, and Aksum
lessons.grammar_note: Nubia, Kush, and Meroe name overlapping things across time: Nubia is the region, Kush the kingdom, and Napata and Meroe its successive capitals.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe two early African civilizations that grew beside major waterways: the Nubian kingdom of Kush along the upper Nile, and Aksum near the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa. You will be able to say what each is known for, how each connected to wider trade, and why both matter for understanding that complex states arose across Africa, not only in Egypt. Warm-up: the Nile flows from south to north, so 'upper' Egypt is in the south. Given that, where would you look on a map for the lands of Kush relative to Egypt? Hold that geography in mind as you read, because the relationship between Egypt and Nubia runs in both directions over the centuries.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: South of Egypt, along the Nile in what is now Sudan, lay Nubia, home to the powerful kingdom of Kush. Kush traded in gold, ivory, and iron, built its own pyramids, and at its height even ruled Egypt. Its capitals moved upriver over time, from Kerma to Napata and finally to Meroe, a city known for ironworking and for its own writing script. Far to the southeast, near the Red Sea, the kingdom of Aksum rose in the highlands of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. Aksum grew rich on trade linking the Mediterranean world with the Indian Ocean, struck its own coins, raised towering carved stone pillars called stelae, and adopted Christianity early. Both states show literate, organized, long-lasting African civilizations deeply tied into trade networks spanning three continents.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Around 750 BCE the Kushite king Piye marched north and conquered Egypt, founding its 25th Dynasty; later Kushite rulers such as Taharqa governed both lands. After losing Egypt, Kush flourished at Meroe for centuries, famous for iron smelting and its many steep pyramids. In the 4th century CE the Aksumite king Ezana converted to Christianity, making Aksum one of the earliest Christian states; its port of Adulis tied it to Rome, Arabia, and India. The Persian writer Mani ranked Aksum among the great powers of his age. The giant Aksumite stelae, the tallest among the largest single stones ever quarried and raised in the ancient world, still stand at the site today.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In which modern countries did Kush and Aksum mostly lie? 2) Name the final capital of Kush, famous for ironworking. 3) What did King Piye do around 750 BCE? 4) Which religion did Aksum adopt under Ezana, and roughly when? 5) Name one thing Aksum is known for building. Answers: 1) Kush was mainly in present-day Sudan; Aksum in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. 2) Meroe. 3) He conquered Egypt and founded its 25th Dynasty. 4) Christianity, in the 4th century CE. 5) Tall carved stone stelae (and it also struck its own coins).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming Nubia was merely a shadow of Egypt. Kush was its own civilization, traded independently, and for a time ruled Egypt itself. Mistake: thinking Christianity reached Africa only with later European contact. Aksum and Nubia were Christian centuries before that, and Ethiopia has one of the world's oldest churches. Mistake: confusing Kush's shifting capitals. Remember the order Kerma, Napata, Meroe. Exit: (a) Which African kingdom ruled Egypt as its 25th Dynasty? (b) Name the early Christian kingdom of the Horn that minted its own coins. Answers: Kush, under kings such as Piye and Taharqa; Aksum.

lessons.title: The Bantu migrations
lessons.grammar_note: 'Bantu' names a large family of related languages and the people who speak them, not a single tribe or empire. The 'migration' was a slow spread over many centuries, not one journey.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the Bantu migrations were, why they matter, and how a language family came to stretch across much of the continent. You will be able to describe, in plain terms, how farming, ironworking, and language spread together over a vast area and a very long time. Warm-up: if the people in dozens of distant regions speak clearly related languages, what might that suggest about their shared past? Keep that reasoning in mind, because it is exactly the clue linguists followed to trace this story. This lesson connects the early civilizations you have met to the peopling of central, eastern, and southern Africa, and it helps explain why so much of the continent shares deep cultural roots.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Beginning several thousand years ago, communities speaking early Bantu languages spread out from a homeland near the modern Nigeria-Cameroon border. Over many centuries, in gradual waves rather than one great march, they moved east and south across central, eastern, and southern Africa. They did not travel empty-handed: they carried farming of crops such as yams and later grains, knowledge of ironworking, and pottery styles that archaeologists can trace. As they settled, they mixed with existing hunter-gatherer and herding peoples, and their languages took root and diversified. Today hundreds of related Bantu languages, including Swahili, Zulu, Kikongo, and Shona, are spoken by a large share of Africa's population. The migrations are one of the great movements in human history and a foundation for later kingdoms across the continent's center and south.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Linguists reconstruct the Bantu homeland in the grasslands and forest edges of present-day Cameroon and eastern Nigeria. One major route ran east toward the Great Lakes region, another south through the Congo basin and on toward southern Africa. The spread of ironworking is closely associated with this expansion, giving communities better tools and weapons. Archaeological pottery traditions, along with the family tree of the languages themselves, let scholars map the routes and rough timing, with the expansion unfolding across the last few thousand years and reaching southern Africa in the early centuries CE. There is no single conquering hero here; the story is told through comparative linguistics and archaeology rather than the deeds of named kings, which makes it a powerful case of history reconstructed from patient evidence.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Roughly where was the Bantu homeland? 2) In which directions did the migrations mostly go? 3) Name two things that spread along with the people. 4) Name two modern Bantu languages. 5) Was this a single journey or a long, gradual process? Answers: 1) Near the present-day Nigeria-Cameroon border. 2) East and south across central, eastern, and southern Africa. 3) Any two of: farming of crops, ironworking, pottery styles. 4) Any two of: Swahili, Zulu, Kikongo, Shona. 5) A long, gradual process over many centuries, not one journey.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: picturing a single army or one rapid march. The expansion was slow, in waves, over a very long span. Mistake: treating 'Bantu' as one tribe. It is a wide family of related languages and peoples. Mistake: imagining newcomers to empty land; they met and mixed with peoples already present, such as hunter-gatherers and herders. Exit: (a) 'Bantu' refers to a family of what? (b) Name one technology that spread with the migrations. Answers: a family of related languages (and the peoples who speak them); ironworking (or farming, or pottery traditions).

lessons.title: Gold, salt, and scholarship: the West African empires and the trans-Saharan trade
lessons.grammar_note: Ghana, Mali, and Songhai are the names of medieval empires in the western Sahel. The modern country of Ghana took its name in honor of the old empire but sits in a different place.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the three great empires of the western Sahel, Ghana, Mali, and Songhai, and explain how trade across the Sahara made them wealthy and famous. You will be able to place Mansa Musa, the city of Timbuktu, and the gold-for-salt exchange in a clear sequence. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what did West Africa chiefly send north across the desert, and what did it receive in return? Hold that exchange in mind, because control of it is the thread running through all three empires. This lesson shows wealthy, literate, well-governed states at the heart of a trade network that linked West Africa to North Africa, the Mediterranean, and the wider Islamic world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Between the forest and the Sahara lies the Sahel, a belt of grassland that became the home of successive empires grown rich on trade. Caravans carried West African gold north across the desert and brought back salt, which was scarce and vital in the south, along with copper, cloth, and books. The empire of Ghana, the Soninke state of Wagadou, rose first by taxing this trade. Mali followed, founded in the 13th century and expanding into one of the largest and richest empires of its age. Songhai rose last, centered on the city of Gao, and grew into the largest of the three. Cities such as Timbuktu and Djenne became centers of commerce and of Islamic learning, with libraries and universities drawing scholars from far away. These were states of law, taxation, and scholarship.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: The empire of Mali is linked to Sundiata, its founding hero, and above all to Mansa Musa, whose pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 was so laden with gold that his generosity is remembered all along the route; he brought scholars and architects home and made Timbuktu shine. Songhai reached its height under the conqueror Sunni Ali and the administrator Askia Muhammad, who organized the empire and promoted learning. Timbuktu's scholars produced and copied thousands of manuscripts on law, science, and history, many of which survive. Songhai fell in 1591 when a Moroccan army, carrying firearms across the desert, defeated it at the Battle of Tondibi, ending the long era of the great Sahelian empires.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List the three empires in the order they rose to power. 2) What two goods were at the heart of the trans-Saharan trade? 3) Who was Mansa Musa, and what is he famous for? 4) Name a city known as a center of Islamic learning. 5) What ended the Songhai Empire in 1591? Answers: 1) Ghana, then Mali, then Songhai. 2) Gold (from the south) and salt (from the Sahara). 3) The emperor of Mali, famous for his gold-laden 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca. 4) Timbuktu (or Djenne). 5) A Moroccan invasion, which won the Battle of Tondibi using firearms.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the medieval Ghana Empire with the modern country of Ghana; they share a name but sit in different places. Mistake: imagining these empires as isolated. They were deeply connected by trade and scholarship to North Africa and the Islamic world. Mistake: thinking Timbuktu was only a trading post. It was a renowned center of books and learning. Exit: (a) Name the empire famous for Mansa Musa. (b) What did West African gold mainly buy from the north? Answers: Mali; salt (along with copper, cloth, and books).

questions.prompt: The main dispersal of modern humans out of Africa is usually dated to roughly…
questions.explanation: Homo sapiens arose in Africa far earlier, but the major spread to other continents is placed around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago.

questions.prompt: The final capital of Kush, famous for ironworking and steep pyramids, was…
questions.explanation: Kush's capital moved from Kerma to Napata and finally to Meroe, a noted ironworking center.

questions.prompt: The Bantu migrations spread, along with people, chiefly which combination?
questions.explanation: The expansion carried crop farming, ironworking, and distinctive pottery across central, eastern, and southern Africa.

questions.prompt: Which empire rose first in the western Sahel, taxing the gold-and-salt trade?
questions.explanation: The Soninke empire of Ghana, or Wagadou, rose first, before Mali and then Songhai.

questions.prompt: Mansa Musa, remembered for his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, ruled which empire?
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa was the emperor of Mali, whose gold-laden hajj became legendary.

questions.prompt: Aksum, in the Horn of Africa, is especially known for all of the following EXCEPT…
options: building the Great Pyramid of Giza
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramid is in Egypt; Aksum is known for coins, stelae, and early Christianity under King Ezana.

lessons.title: The Indian Ocean world: the Swahili coast and Great Zimbabwe
lessons.grammar_note: 'Swahili' names both a language and a coastal culture. The word comes from an Arabic term for 'coasts,' reflecting the trade links that shaped it, but the language itself is Bantu at its core.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the trading world of the eastern and southern African coast and interior: the Swahili city-states strung along the Indian Ocean, and the stone city of Great Zimbabwe inland. You will be able to explain how monsoon winds, gold, and cattle tied these places into a wide commercial network reaching Arabia, India, and China. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, who built the great dry-stone walls of Great Zimbabwe, and in roughly which centuries? Hold that in mind, because the gold that flowed through Great Zimbabwe helped make the coastal cities rich. This lesson shows African societies as active, prosperous partners in one of the premodern world's busiest trade systems, not as bystanders on its edge.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Along the East African coast, from Mombasa and Malindi to Kilwa and Zanzibar, grew a chain of Swahili city-states. Their merchants used the predictable monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean to sail to and from Arabia, Persia, India, and even China, exporting gold, ivory, and other goods and importing cloth, beads, and porcelain. Swahili culture blended its Bantu foundation with Arab, Persian, and Indian influences, and many of its people adopted Islam; the stone towns, with their coral-rock houses and mosques, reflected this cosmopolitan wealth. Much of the gold reaching the coast came from the interior, where the Shona-speaking people built Great Zimbabwe, a city of massive mortarless stone walls that was the center of a powerful state controlling cattle and the gold trade. Coast and interior rose together, linked by commerce.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Kilwa, on an island off modern Tanzania, became one of the wealthiest Swahili city-states, with a great mosque and a palace complex; the traveler Ibn Battuta visited in the 14th century and praised the town. Great Zimbabwe flourished from roughly the 11th to the 15th century; its Great Enclosure, with walls built of fitted stone without mortar, is among the largest ancient structures south of the Sahara, and carved soapstone birds found there became national symbols. Mapungubwe, an earlier state to the south, preceded it. When Portuguese ships rounded Africa around 1500, they found these cities already thriving and attacked and taxed several, disrupting an ancient trading order they had not created.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name two Swahili coastal cities. 2) What natural feature made Indian Ocean sailing predictable? 3) Who built Great Zimbabwe? 4) What made Great Zimbabwe's walls unusual in construction? 5) What was the main valuable that linked the interior to the coast? Answers: 1) Any two of Mombasa, Malindi, Kilwa, Zanzibar. 2) The seasonal monsoon winds. 3) Shona-speaking people. 4) They were built of fitted stone without mortar (dry-stone). 5) Gold (along with ivory).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking foreigners built Great Zimbabwe. This false idea was pushed in the colonial era; the builders were local Shona ancestors, a point confirmed by archaeology. Mistake: picturing the Swahili coast as simply an Arab colony. It was an African culture, Bantu at its core, that absorbed and traded with many partners. Mistake: assuming the Portuguese opened Indian Ocean trade; it was ancient and thriving before they arrived. Exit: (a) Name the wealthy island city-state visited by Ibn Battuta. (b) Who built Great Zimbabwe? Answers: Kilwa; the Shona-speaking people of the interior.

lessons.title: Kingdoms of the forest and savanna: Kongo, Benin, and Asante
lessons.grammar_note: 'Benin' here means the historical Kingdom of Benin in present-day Nigeria, not the modern country called Benin next door. The famous 'Benin Bronzes' come from the kingdom.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe three influential states of central and West Africa's forest and savanna zones: the Kingdom of Kongo, the Kingdom of Benin, and the Asante Empire. You will be able to name what each is known for, from Kongo's early diplomacy with Portugal to Benin's renowned artworks and Asante's Golden Stool. Warm-up: the famous 'Benin Bronzes' are named after a kingdom, not the modern country of Benin. Where, in today's map, was that kingdom? Keep the distinction clear as you read. This lesson rounds out the picture of organized African states with their own courts, armies, art, and traditions of rule, the kind of complexity the 'no history' myth tried to deny.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: South of the great Sahelian empires, in the forests and savannas of central and West Africa, powerful kingdoms governed millions. The Kingdom of Kongo, in central Africa near the mouth of the Congo River, was a well-organized state with a capital at Mbanza Kongo; it opened relations with Portugal in the late 15th century and some of its rulers adopted Christianity. In the forests of what is now southern Nigeria, the Kingdom of Benin, ruled by a sovereign called the Oba, built a great walled capital and produced magnificent cast-metal and ivory artworks. To the west, among the Akan of present-day Ghana, the Asante Empire united many peoples around the sacred Golden Stool and the capital of Kumasi. Each had its own institutions of kingship, law, and craftsmanship.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Portuguese ships reached the Kingdom of Kongo in 1483; its ruler Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptized, and his son Afonso I corresponded with Portugal and Rome, later protesting the growing slave trade that was harming his kingdom. The Kingdom of Benin's artists created the Benin Bronzes, thousands of plaques and sculptures adorning the royal palace; British forces looted them during a punitive expedition in 1897, and their return is debated to this day. The Asante Empire, founded around 1700 under Osei Tutu and his adviser Okomfo Anokye, centered on the Golden Stool, a symbol said to hold the soul of the nation; the Asante fought a series of wars against the British before finally being annexed in the early 20th century.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Near which river was the Kingdom of Kongo centered? 2) What is the ruler of Benin called? 3) What are the Benin Bronzes, and what happened to many of them in 1897? 4) What sacred object was central to the Asante Empire? 5) Which Kongo king protested the slave trade's harm? Answers: 1) The Congo River (its capital was Mbanza Kongo). 2) The Oba. 3) Cast-metal and ivory artworks from the royal palace; British forces looted them in a punitive expedition. 4) The Golden Stool. 5) Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the historical Kingdom of Benin (in modern Nigeria) with the modern country of Benin next door. Mistake: assuming Africa only reacted to outsiders. Kongo conducted its own diplomacy and correspondence with Europe. Mistake: thinking the Benin Bronzes were a European gift or import; they were African masterworks, later looted. Exit: (a) Name the central African kingdom whose king Afonso I wrote to Portugal. (b) What sacred object symbolized the Asante nation? Answers: the Kingdom of Kongo; the Golden Stool.

lessons.title: The Atlantic slave trade and its impact
lessons.grammar_note: Write about enslaved people as people, not as cargo. Phrases like 'enslaved Africans' keep their humanity in view; older sources that call them 'slaves' or goods reflect the dehumanizing language of the trade itself.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the transatlantic slave trade was, how it worked, its vast human scale, and the lasting damage it did to African societies. You will be able to describe the triangular trade and the Middle Passage, and to discuss impacts both in Africa and across the Atlantic world with care and accuracy. Warm-up: in the last lesson, the Kongo king Afonso I protested a trade that was harming his kingdom. What trade do you think he meant, and why would a ruler fear it? Approach this difficult subject soberly; it is one of the largest forced migrations in history, and understanding it honestly is part of treating the people caught in it with respect.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: From the 16th to the 19th century, European traders shipped millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to labor on plantations and in mines in the Americas. The system is often sketched as a triangular trade: manufactured goods and firearms went from Europe to the African coast; enslaved people were carried across the Atlantic in the horrific voyage called the Middle Passage; and plantation products such as sugar, tobacco, and cotton returned to Europe. Captives were seized in raids and wars, often far inland, and sold at coastal forts. The scale was immense, and the human cost beyond counting: families destroyed, communities depopulated, and vast suffering and death in the crossing itself. The trade enriched European and American economies while inflicting deep and lasting harm on much of Africa.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: Historians estimate that roughly twelve million or more Africans were forced onto slave ships, with a large share dying during capture, transport, or the Middle Passage. The demand for captives intensified warfare and raiding in parts of West and central Africa, and some coastal states, such as Dahomey and Oyo, became deeply involved in supplying the trade, while others, like Kongo, were torn apart by it. The movement to abolish the trade grew in the late 18th and early 19th centuries; Britain outlawed the trade in 1807 and slavery in its empire in the 1830s, with other nations following, though illegal shipments continued for decades. The trade's legacies include the African diaspora of the Americas and enduring economic and demographic scars at home.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Across which ocean were enslaved Africans forcibly shipped? 2) What was the Middle Passage? 3) Name the three legs of the triangular trade. 4) Roughly how many Africans are estimated to have been forced onto slave ships? 5) When did Britain outlaw the slave trade? Answers: 1) The Atlantic. 2) The brutal transatlantic voyage carrying captured Africans to the Americas. 3) Goods and firearms from Europe to Africa; enslaved people from Africa to the Americas; plantation products back to Europe. 4) Roughly twelve million or more. 5) In 1807 (slavery in its empire followed in the 1830s).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using the language of cargo for human beings; speak of enslaved people, not goods. Mistake: treating the trade as a minor side note; it was one of history's largest forced migrations, with consequences still felt today. Mistake: flattening African involvement into a single story; some states resisted or were destroyed by the trade while others took part, and ordinary people were its victims, not its planners. Exit: (a) Name the transatlantic voyage endured by captured Africans. (b) Name one lasting legacy of the trade. Answers: the Middle Passage; the African diaspora in the Americas (and lasting demographic and economic harm in Africa).

lessons.title: The Scramble for Africa, independence, and the modern continent
lessons.grammar_note: 'Decolonization' is the process by which colonies became independent states. 'Pan-Africanism' is the idea that African peoples share common interests and should cooperate or unite.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how European powers colonized nearly all of Africa in a few decades, how Africans resisted, and how they won independence and built the states of today. You will be able to connect the Berlin Conference, colonial rule, liberation movements, and modern institutions in a clear line. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, where was the 1884-1885 conference that set the rules for partitioning Africa, and what colony became independent first in 1957? Keep both answers in view, because this lesson runs from conquest to freedom. It is the culmination of the course: the attempt to seize a continent, the determined struggle against it, and the emergence of dozens of sovereign African nations with their own voices in the world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For most of history Europeans held only coastal footholds in Africa. Then, in the late 19th century, rivalry and new weapons and medicines drove a rapid 'Scramble for Africa.' At the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885, European powers agreed on rules for dividing the continent, drawing borders that ignored existing nations and peoples. Within about three decades nearly all of Africa was under colonial rule, and colonizers extracted resources and labor while suppressing self-government. Africans resisted throughout, by arms and by organizing. After the Second World War the demand for freedom became unstoppable: through protest, negotiation, and sometimes war, colony after colony won independence, especially around 1960. The new nations then faced the hard work of building states, economies, and unity on borders they had not chosen.

sections.heading: Key events & figures
sections.text: By 1914 almost all of Africa was colonized; the main exceptions were Ethiopia and Liberia. Ethiopia famously defeated an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 under Emperor Menelik II, becoming a symbol of African resistance. Armed resistance elsewhere included Samori Ture in West Africa and the Maji Maji uprising in East Africa. The independence era broke open in 1957 when Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first sub-Saharan colony to gain independence; 1960 saw some seventeen African nations become independent in a single 'Year of Africa.' In South Africa the apartheid system of racial rule fell only in 1994, when Nelson Mandela was elected president. The Organisation of African Unity, founded in 1963, later became the African Union.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What was agreed at the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885? 2) Which two states remained largely uncolonized by 1914? 3) What happened at the Battle of Adwa in 1896? 4) Which country became independent first in sub-Saharan Africa, and under whom? 5) What ended in South Africa in 1994? Answers: 1) Rules for European powers to partition Africa. 2) Ethiopia and Liberia. 3) Ethiopia defeated an Italian invasion under Menelik II. 4) Ghana, under Kwame Nkrumah, in 1957. 5) Apartheid, with Nelson Mandela's election as president.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming Africans accepted colonization passively; resistance was constant, from Adwa to Maji Maji to mass political movements. Mistake: thinking colonial borders followed African nations; they were drawn in Europe and often split or merged peoples, causing lasting tensions. Mistake: treating independence as the end of the story; building nations and institutions on those inherited borders is ongoing work. Exit: (a) Name the 1896 battle where Ethiopia defeated Italy. (b) Who became South Africa's president in 1994 as apartheid ended? Answers: the Battle of Adwa; Nelson Mandela.
